page: Amazon Web Services m8idb.24xlarge is an eighth-generation general-purpose instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. The server features an Intel x86_64 processor clocked at 3.9 GHz, providing 48 physical cores and 96 dedicated vCPUs with two threads per core. System memory is configured at 384.0 GB, delivering a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU.

Storage is provided by 5,700 GB of bundled local NVMe SSD instance store volumes, designed for low-latency scratch data and high IOPS workloads. The instance does not include a GPU accelerator. Network capabilities are provisioned with a baseline bandwidth of 100 Gbps, facilitating rapid inter-node communication and data ingestion.

The combination of high compute capacity, direct-attached NVMe storage, and 100 Gbps throughput makes the m8idb.24xlarge resource-dense for IO-heavy distributed applications. Because local NVMe disks are ephemeral, workloads requiring state durability must manage persistence across redundant nodes or cloud storage volumes. Primary workload fits include high-performance relational databases, distributed caching clusters, big data analytics engines, and large-scale compilation tasks.
description: Amazon Web Services m8idb.24xlarge is an eighth-generation general-purpose instance running on the AWS Nitro hypervisor and Intel x86_64 hardware. Operating at a 3.9 GHz clock frequency, it supplies 96 dedicated vCPUs across 48 physical cores alongside 384.0 GB of memory, preserving a standard 1:4 compute-to-RAM allocation. Storage needs are met with 5,700 GB of direct-attached NVMe SSD instance storage for high-speed ephemeral operations, complemented by a 100 Gbps baseline network connection. The platform lacks discrete GPU acceleration. The large local storage footprint paired with extensive network bandwidth provides qualitative cost efficiency for clustered environments that rely heavily on rapid intermediate data staging rather than external network block storage. It is structured for demanding production workloads including high-transaction databases, real-time analytics engines, in-memory key-value caches, and distributed build pipelines.
